1	# Offline Autonomous Node Coordination
2	
3	Minimal backend baseline for autonomous nodes that must keep working during long network outages and later reconcile state with explainable rules.
4	
5	Requires Python 3.11 or newer and has no third-party runtime dependencies.
6	
7	```bash
8	python -m offline_coordination status
9	python -m offline_coordination recovery check LEDGER [LEDGER ...]
10	python -m offline_coordination recovery run LEDGER [LEDGER ...] --keyring KEYRING --ticket TICKET --moment MOMENT --audit AUDIT
11	python -m offline_coordination recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]
12	python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
13	```
14	
15	The baseline exposes a local status command plus offline ledger recovery operations. Persistent state is available via `offline_coordination.storage` and an append-only hash-chained audit log via `offline_coordination.audit`. Replication, conflict policies, security boundaries, observability, and network services are intentionally left for subsequent tasks.
16	
17	## Ledger recovery
18	
19	`offline_coordination.replication.recover_ledger(path)` settles one interrupted ledger transaction. Its `clean` result (no recovery intent) reports the SHA-256 of the current ledger bytes, lowercase hex, or `None` when the path is missing.
20	
21	Two batch entry points operate on an explicit, non-empty list of distinct, non-empty ledger paths, validated in full before any file is read or modified (`TypeError` for container/element type faults, `ValueError` for an empty list, empty path or duplicate):
22	
23	- `inspect_recovery(paths)` — read-only diagnostics. Each report carries `path`, `status`, `phase`, `digest`, `artifacts`, `action` and `error`: `clean` when no intent exists, `pending` with the suggested action (`rollback`/`complete`) and candidate/predecessor existence, digest-match and completeness when an intent is valid, `blocked`/`corrupt` when the intent or a necessary artifact is invalid, and `failed`/`os-error` when reading fails. Nothing is created, modified or deleted, and random artifacts are never scanned.
24	- `recover_many(paths)` — controlled batch recovery. Each ledger is recovered via `recover_ledger` in order; one failure never stops or rolls back the others. Successful items keep the `clean`/`rolled-back`/`completed` statuses; a `CorruptRecoveryError` becomes a `blocked`/`corrupt` item and an `OSError` a `failed`/`os-error` item, leaving enough intent and artifacts behind for an independent retry.
25	
26	The module entry points `recovery check` and `recovery run` wrap these: they print exactly one line of compact UTF-8 JSON with recursively sorted keys, exit 0 when every ledger succeeds, 1 when any ledger is blocked or failed, and 2 on syntax or argument errors.
27	
28	## Authorized recovery and the recovery audit
29	
30	`offline_coordination.replication.recover_authorized(paths, keyring, ticket, moment, audit)` adds an authorization boundary and a durable operation audit around the same batch recovery. The ticket is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline, space or any other byte after the closing brace; it carries exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload carries exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `nonce`, `notBefore`, `notAfter` and the ordered `paths`, and the signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload encoding, verified against the keyring (the same version/secret/validity/revocation rules as `apply_signed_remote`, keys selected by exact issuer and version). The command paths must equal the ticket paths item for item — never expanded, reordered or normalized. Unknown credentials, a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key or ticket, a path mismatch and a signature mismatch all raise `AuthenticationError` before any ledger is read, so a failed authorization creates no audit record, consumes no nonce and leaves no temporary file. An old-style ticket carrying a trailing newline (or any other non-canonical encoding) raises `ValueError`; field type faults raise `TypeError` (a `bool` never poses as `moment`); a malformed ticket key set, nonce, validity interval or signature format raises `ValueError`.
31	
32	Once authorized, the batch runs in the `recover_many` order with the same per-ledger isolation and the same public item structure, and every step is recorded at the audit path as an append-only canonical JSONL hash chain, each record written, flushed and synced before the step it gates: a `batch` header on the first use of a nonce (binding the ticket digest, issuer and ordered paths), then a `before` record (original digest, phase, planned action) and an `after` record (new digest, status, failure category) per ledger. An `OSError` while reading the audit or writing, flushing or syncing a record propagates unchanged and leaves a consistent, retryable chain prefix. Re-entering with the same nonce and the same ticket reuses the recorded results and only continues the paths not yet settled — a process interrupted after a recovery but before its result record is completed from the recorded action and digests, without repeating side effects. The same nonce bound to a different ticket raises `ReplayError` (a `ValueError`) without modifying any file; a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError` (a `ValueError`).
33	
34	`export_recovery_audit(path, after=0, limit=100)` pages the chain read-only (`after`/`complete`/`next`/`records`), validating the whole chain and treating a missing audit as an empty chain. The module entry point `recovery run` requires the four explicit materials `--keyring`, `--ticket`, `--moment` and `--audit` and exits 0 on success, 1 on ledger failures and 2 on authorization or argument errors; `recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]` prints one page of the chain.
35	
36	`export_recovery_checkpoint(audit, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` adds an offline signature anchor that a later full-history replacement cannot recompute. It reads and validates the whole chain read-only and returns `bytes`: one compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline or any other trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`. The payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `lastSeq`, `moment`, `tail` and `version` (integer 1) — `lastSeq` is the last chain seq (0 for a missing audit) and `tail` the last record hash (the zero hash for an empty chain). `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key the keyring binds to the exact issuer and version, with no fallback; unknown credentials and a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key raise `AuthenticationError`, a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError`, and an `OSError` while reading propagates unchanged.
37	
38	`verify_recovery_page(checkpoint, page, keyring, moment, cursor=None)` verifies a page dict against the checkpoint entirely offline — no file is read and no argument is modified. The checkpoint is parsed and its HMAC verified against the current keyring (exact issuer/version, usable at `moment`, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it); the bound `moment` is part of the signed payload itself. The first call passes no cursor and the page's `after` must be zero; later calls pass `{"digest", "next", "tail"}` built from the previous result, so `after` must equal the cursor `next`, the first record must chain to the cursor `tail`, and the cursor `digest` must equal this checkpoint's SHA-256 digest — a cursor can never resume another checkpoint. Each page's records must be contiguous from `after + 1` (no empty page, gap, reordering, duplicate or predecessor mismatch before the signed end), hash-correct within the page and across the paging boundary, and verification never crosses the signed `lastSeq`. The result carries `digest`, `lastSeq`, `status` and `tail`: reaching the signed tail is `verified`, every earlier page `continue`. An empty checkpoint accepts only an empty page starting at zero and directly reports seq 0, the zero hash and `verified`. Parameter or field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); keyring structure or format faults raise `ValueError`; checkpoint faults raise `InvalidRecoveryCheckpointError` and page or cursor faults raise `InvalidRecoveryPageError`, both `ValueError` subclasses.
39	
40	`verify_recovery_checkpoints(items, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of checkpoints offline and never reads a file. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id`, the `checkpoint` bytes and the non-empty `pages` list holding that checkpoint's paging dicts in export order. The batch is validated in full before any item is verified — container, field or element type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id, a wrong item key set or an empty page list raises `ValueError` (keyring and `moment`, a non-negative non-bool int, keep their usual classification). Each item is then handled in input order and in isolation: its pages are walked from a zero cursor through the exact `verify_recovery_page` rules, each cursor bound to the same checkpoint digest and the previous page's chain tail; keys are selected by the checkpoint's own exact issuer and version with no fallback, so checkpoints signed before and after a key rotation verify independently in one batch while the keyring retains both versions. Pages that reach the signed `lastSeq` must end there (any further page is a page fault); pages exhausted earlier are `incomplete` and keep the verified boundary. The result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items`, `version` (integer 1); each item report carries `id`, the checkpoint `digest`, the signed `issuer` and `keyVersion` (both null when the checkpoint does not parse), the verified `boundary` (`{"lastSeq","tail"}`, null when nothing was verified), a `status` of `verified`, `incomplete`, `invalid-checkpoint`, `invalid-page` or `unauthenticated`, and an `error` message (null exactly when verified). Only a batch-level or keyring-level fault raises — one item's failure never stops the later items, and no input is modified.
41	
42	`adjudicate_recovery(items, policy, keyring, moment)` aggregates those per-site verifications into one offline verdict, reading no file and modifying no input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and `attestation` bytes. An attestation is a compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `site`, `keyVersion` and `result` with no extra fields, where `result` has the single-item batch verification shape (`boundary`, `digest`, `error`, `id`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `status`). Every legal single-item result is accepted: a `verified` result always carries identity, a positive key version and a boundary, while a non-verified result may carry a null issuer/keyVersion (when the checkpoint did not parse) or a null boundary — its identity, digest, boundary and status are preserved — and only a `verified` result may count. `policy` is `{"batch", "sites", "threshold"}`: the authorized batch id, a positive threshold no greater than the site count, and a non-empty map of each authorized site to its non-empty set of allowed positive key versions; `keyring` and `moment` keep their existing structure, validity and revocation rules. The signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key selected by the exact site and version, with no fallback.
43	
44	A batch or identity that is not authorized, unavailable/revoked/not-yet-valid/expired credentials, a wrong signature or a non-verified result each reject the packet with a fixed reason (`unauthorized-batch`, `unauthorized-site`, `unauthorized-version`, `credential-unavailable`, `revoked`, `not-yet-valid`, `expired`, `bad-signature`, `not-verified`) and never count; one packet with illegal encoding, key sets or fields is rejected alone as `invalid-attestation` without blocking the others. For one site an identical valid packet — the complete embedded result equal on every field — counts once and extra copies are `duplicate`; any different valid result (even one sharing digest and boundary) is a self-`contradiction`. Valid packets from different sites must agree on both digest and boundary — any disagreement is a fork a majority cannot outvote. The return is one canonical compact JSON object with the top-level keys `boundary`, `digest`, `items`, `status`, `threshold` and `version` (integer 1), no trailing byte: any contradiction or cross-site fork is `conflicted` with a null digest and boundary; a unique agreed result attested by at least the threshold of distinct sites is `accepted`; everything else is `insufficient`. Every packet stays in `items` — sorted stably by site then id — with its identity, conclusion (`valid`/`invalid`/`duplicate`/`contradiction`), fixed reason (null only for valid) and boundary, and the verdict does not depend on input order. Parameter, container or public field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an empty list, duplicate id or illegal threshold, site or version rule raises `ValueError`.
45	
46	`export_recovery_verdict(verdict, policy, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` signs that aggregate verdict for offline handover, reading and writing no file. It takes the canonical compact verdict bytes `adjudicate_recovery` returned, the same policy, a keyring, the signing issuer, key version and moment. It returns one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest` and the complete `verdict`. The policy is canonicalized — sites in ascending order and each site's versions as an ascending array, all keys recursively sorted into compact UTF-8 — and `policyDigest` is its SHA-256; `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback. Unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`. A non-bytes verdict or a wrong field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); a bad issuer, version or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal verdict raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictError`.
47	
48	`verify_recovery_verdict(proof, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies such a handover proof entirely offline from just the proof, the policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It recomputes the two digests, checks the batch, threshold, signing moment, proof/verdict structure and digest bindings, and re-checks the credentials against the current keyring (exact issuer/version usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it). It returns a fresh dict keyed `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest`, `verdictDigest`, `status`, `digest`, `boundary`, `items` and `version` (integer 1). A non-bytes proof or a wrong public field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an illegal policy, identifier, version or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal verdict argument to `export_recovery_verdict` raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictError`, while a bad proof structure — including an illegal verdict structure, field type or canonical encoding bound into the payload — a digest mismatch or a batch/threshold binding fault raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictProofError` (both subclass `ValueError`); a bad signature or current credentials raise `AuthenticationError`.
49	
50	`verify_recovery_verdicts(items, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of those handover proofs offline and never reads or writes a file or modifies an input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and the `proof` bytes. The batch is validated in full — container, element or public field type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or a wrong item key set raises `ValueError` — together with the shared `policy`, `keyring` and `moment`, which keep the single-entry validation and exception classification (a non-negative non-bool int) before any proof is verified; only such a batch-level fault raises. Each item is then verified independently, in strict input order, through the exact `verify_recovery_verdict` rules: one proof's failure never stops a later item or changes an earlier report, and each proof selects its key by its own exact issuer and key version with no fallback, so proofs bound to different issuers or rotations coexist in one batch. A currently revoked, not-yet-valid, expired or missing credential or a wrong signature makes that item `unauthenticated`; an illegal encoding, key set, field, digest, batch, threshold, signing moment or embedded verdict makes it `invalid-proof`; a passing proof is `verified`. The top-level result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items` and `version` (integer 1); each item report has the fixed key order `error`, `id`, `result`, `status`, where a verified item keeps `error` null and `result` a fresh copy of exactly the dict the single entry returns, and a failed item keeps a definite, non-empty copy of the original exception text with `result` fixed to null — the identity, digest and boundary of an unauthenticated payload never enter a result. 98	Each certificate is then independently re-checked through the exact single-certificate rules (its canonical shape, the decision and certification-moment bindings and a full re-convergence of its rounds), authorized by the exact signing site and key version against `site_policy` with no key fallback, and authenticated against the current keyring. For one site, certificates with the identical complete convergence result — the plan summary, the overall status and every operation's result, settled round and post-state digest — count once and every extra certificate is a `duplicate`; certificates with different complete results are a `contradiction`. Distinct sites must agree exactly on the plan summary, the overall status and every operation's result, settled round and post-state digest. Any self-contradiction or cross-site difference is `conflicted` with the common result set to null and cannot be outvoted by a majority; a unique complete result attested by at least the threshold of distinct sites is `accepted` and keeps the full convergence result; every other case is `insufficient`.
99	
100	The result is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object (recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved, no trailing byte) carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `certificates` (each certificate digest in the original input order), `common` (the complete shared convergence result, null unless accepted), `commonDigest` (the SHA-256 of the canonical common result, null unless accepted), `decisionDigest` (the SHA-256 of the original fork decision bytes), `issuer`, `keyVersion`, the per-certificate `items` (sorted stably by site then id, each carrying its `certificateDigest`, `convergence`, `conclusion`, `id`, `keyVersion`, `reason` and `site`), `planDigest` (the accepted plan digest, null otherwise), `policyDigest` (the SHA-256 of the canonical site policy), `status` and `version` (integer 1). The signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact adjudicator issuer and version with no fallback; unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired adjudicator credentials raise `AuthenticationError`.
101	
102	`verify_convergence_decision(decision_packet, decision, site_policy, keyring, moment)` re-checks such an adjudication entirely offline from just the packet, the original fork decision bytes, the expected site policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It validates the canonical encoding and key sets, recomputes the fork decision and site policy digests, re-tallies the bound per-certificate items purely from the signed payload (the stable site/id ordering, the original-order certificate digest bindings, the same-site duplicate/contradiction markings, cross-site agreement, the threshold, the plan digest and the common result and digest), and checks the HMAC-SHA256 against the key the current keyring binds to the payload's exact issuer and version, usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it. On success it returns a fresh mapping keyed `certificates`, `common`, `commonDigest`, `convergenceDecisionDigest` (the SHA-256 of the packet), `decisionDigest` (the bound fork decision digest), `issuer`, `items`, `keyVersion`, `planDigest`, `policyDigest`, `status` and `version` (integer 1). A non-bytes argument or a wrong public field type raises `TypeError` (a `bool` never poses as an int); an empty value, a duplicate id or an illegal site policy, threshold, moment, site or version raises `ValueError`; an illegal packet structure or binding raises `InvalidConvergenceDecisionError` (a `ValueError` subclass); unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials or a wrong signature raise `AuthenticationError`.
103	
104	`verify_convergence_decisions(items, decision, site_policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a non-empty batch of those adjudications offline and in strict input order, in isolation. Each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and the `decision` packet bytes; the batch and the shared fork decision, site policy, keyring and moment are validated in full before any packet is verified, so only a batch-level fault raises (container/field faults `TypeError`; an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or a wrong item key set `ValueError`). Each packet is then reported in input order as `verified`, `invalid` or `unauthenticated` with the fixed key order `error`, `id`, `result` and `status`; a failed item keeps a definite, non-empty copy of the original exception text and a null result, and the identity of an unauthenticated payload never enters a result. The top-level result has the fixed keys `items` and `version` (integer 1); repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results. The existing convergence certificate, plan, confirmation and batch interfaces, and the module commands, are unchanged.
105	
106	
107	## Supersession chains over convergence decisions
108	
109	`supersede_decision(predecessor, evidence, decision, policy, old_policy, new_policy, keyring, moment, effective_at, issuer, version)` issues one signed successor packet that supersedes an existing convergence decision (the chain root) or the previous successor. `predecessor` is either packet; `evidence` is the stage's non-empty certificate/rounds list. The evidence sequence must have the predecessor as a strict prefix — a first successor keeps the root's certificates and ids in order, a later successor keeps every prior evidence item verbatim, so history is never deleted, changed or reordered; with an unchanged policy at least one new item is required, while a rotation may re-seal the same sequence. `decision`/`policy` are the original fork decision and shared fork policy, and `old_policy`/`new_policy` carry exactly `sites`, `threshold` and a positive integer `policyVersion`: unchanged sites and threshold keep the version, any change increments it by exactly one, and the root, plan and settled operations never change. The new verdict is recomputed from scratch from the full evidence: supplemental evidence moves `insufficient` to `accepted` or `conflicted`, an `accepted` verdict only keeps the identical common result or advances to `conflicted` (it never falls back to `insufficient` or swaps conclusions), and a `conflicted` verdict can never be masked by a later majority. The effective moment never moves backwards; the successor sealer and key version must be authorized by both policies and the credential must be usable both at `effective_at` and at the issuance `moment` (the same must hold for every evidence credential, or the settled verdict would differ at verify time). The packet is canonical compact UTF-8 JSON with exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds the root digest, predecessor digest, height, the full recomputed verdict (certificate digests in original order, items sorted by site then id, status, common result/digest and plan digest), the raw evidence increment (bytes carried as lowercase hex), the old/new policy digests, the policy version, the effective moment, the issuer and key version and `version` (integer 1), signed with HMAC-SHA256 under the exact issuer/version key. Parameter or field type faults raise `TypeError`; an empty value, duplicate id, illegal version or backwards moment raises `ValueError`; a malformed root raises `InvalidConvergenceDecisionError`; a malformed successor or any broken chain rule raises `InvalidChainError`; an identity the policies do not authorize raises `InvalidChainError`; a signature or credential fault raises `AuthenticationError`.
110	
111	`verify_decision_chain(root, successors, decision, policy, policies, keyring, moment)` verifies one chain hop by hop, entirely offline, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. `policies` provides one versioned site policy per stage (the root policy plus one per successor). The root is verified under the first policy's sites and threshold; every successor re-recomputes its verdict from the bound full evidence under its new policy at the hop's effective moment, re-checks the root, predecessor and height links, the old/new policy digests and version step, the non-decreasing effective moment and the append-only evidence prefix, re-applies the verdict state machine and dual-policy sealer authorization, requires the settled verdict to still hold with credentials usable at `moment`, and verifies the HMAC. It returns a fresh mapping with exactly `rootDigest`, `headDigest`, `height` (0 for a bare root), `policyVersion` and `status`; a bad root raises `InvalidConvergenceDecisionError`, a bad successor `InvalidChainError` and a signature or credential fault `AuthenticationError`.
112	
113	`verify_decision_chains(items, decision, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch offline. Each item holds exactly a unique `id`, its `roots` packet, its ordered `successors` packets and its per-stage `policies`; the batch and shared materials are pre-validated in full, so only batch-level faults raise (container/field faults `TypeError`; an empty list, empty or duplicate id or wrong key set `ValueError`). Each chain is then reported in strict input order, in isolation, as `verified`, `invalid` or `unauthenticated` with the fixed key order `error`, `id`, `result` and `status`. One predecessor digest pointing at two distinct successor digests is a fork; a mere prefix extension (one chain growing longer along the same packets) is not. Every verified chain crossing a forking edge is reclassified `conflicted` with its verified result retained; chains that were invalid or unauthenticated are never reclassified. The result has the fixed keys `items` and `version` (integer 1).
114	
115	`seal_decision_head(items, target, decision, policy, keyring, moment, issuer, version)` seals a stable anchor only for the `target` chain within the batch that is `verified` (not conflicted by a fork), whose head is `accepted`. The anchor binds the target's root digest, head digest and height together with the head policy digest, head policy version and sealing moment and is signed under the exact issuer/version key; sealing a batch that is not entirely pre-validated, an unknown or empty target, a non-accepted/forked target or an illegal version raises `ValueError`, and a credential fault raises `AuthenticationError`. `verify_decision_head(anchor, items, target, decision, policy, keyring, moment)` re-checks the anchor structurally and its HMAC against the current key, re-runs the original batch and confirms the target still verifies, is accepted and unforked, and that every bound digest, height and version still matches; it returns `rootDigest`, `headDigest`, `height`, `policyDigest`, `policyVersion` and `anchorDigest`. A bad anchor raises `InvalidAnchorError` (a `ValueError` subclass); a batch fault raises the underlying `InvalidConvergenceDecisionError` or `InvalidChainError`; a signature or credential fault raises `AuthenticationError`. The adjudication, certificate, recovery command and `status` interfaces are unchanged and no new command-line entry is added.
116	
117	## Pruning multi-round convergence archives
118	
119	`plan_chain_prune(paths, checkpoint, decision, policy, keyring, moment)` builds a read-only signed plan for trimming persisted convergence archives, reading the archive files but never modifying, creating or deleting them. `paths` is an explicit, non-empty list of distinct file paths; each archive is one version-1 canonical JSON object (recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved, exactly one trailing `\n`) carrying exactly `project` (a unique non-empty identifier), `certificate` and the ordered `rounds` (each `{confirmation, seq}`, numbered consecutively from one), with the certificate and every confirmation carried as non-empty lowercase hex bytes. The sealing `checkpoint` is a `seal_chain_checkpoint` packet authenticated against the current keyring through the exact `verify_chain_suffix` rules (exact issuer/version, usable at `moment`, no fallback). An archive is eligible for pruning only when its certificate digest is part of the checkpoint's pruned evidence prefix and its whole round group re-verifies through the exact `verify_fork_convergence` rules against `decision`, `policy` and `keyring` at `moment`; non-eligible archives are retained and when nothing is eligible a `ValueError` is raised. The result is one canonical compact `{payload, signature}` object with no trailing byte; the payload binds exactly `checkpoint` (its SHA-256), `delete` (eligible projects ascending), `retain` (the SHA-256 of every retained archive's bytes, ascending), `source` and `target` (each a map from an eligible project to the digest of its archive bytes before pruning and of its trimmed project-marker archive afterwards) and `version` (integer 1). It carries no moment or project identifier of its own and is signed with the checkpoint's own exact issuer/key, so equal arguments produce byte-identical plans. Container/field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an empty/duplicate path or project, a wrong key set or an illegal version raises `ValueError`; a missing archive raises `FileNotFoundError`; an illegal archive or checkpoint raises `InvalidPruneError`; credential and signature faults raise `AuthenticationError`.
120	
121	`prune_chain_archives(items, keyring)` executes the plans in one controlled batch. Each item holds exactly a unique non-empty `id`, an archive `path`, the signed `plan`, the sealing `checkpoint` and a `header` naming the exact signing `issuer`/`keyVersion` (the checkpoint sealer) and the non-negative prune `moment`; the batch structure and keyring are validated first. Each item then runs in strict input order and full isolation: bad credentials, malformed plans or checkpoints and stale archives are recorded for that item alone, the archive is left unchanged and the batch continues. When the archive at `path` hashes to the plan's source digest for its project, the planned trimmed target (one canonical `{project, version}` marker ending in one `\n`, the certificate and all round bytes gone) is installed in a crash-safe two-phase transaction, and the receipt status is `pruned`; when the archive already hashes to the target digest nothing is written and the status is `duplicate`; any other content records `StalePruneError`. An `OSError` raised while writing, flushing, syncing a file or directory, replacing or deleting is recorded for that item with its original text and leaves the retryable transaction material in place. The transaction uses only same-directory files — a unique candidate, the hard-linked predecessor and the `path + ".prune.txn"` intent — whose only phases are `prepared` and `installed`; unrelated files are never scanned or touched. The batch returns, in input order, fresh dicts keyed `id`, `receipt` and `error`. The receipt is one canonical compact `{payload, signature}` object binding the `status`, the complete plan, the `checkpoint` digest, `beforeDigest`/`afterDigest` (equal for a duplicate), the full `delete` and `retain` digests, the prune `moment` and `version` 1, signed under the exact header key. The first completion and a same-plan re-entry (an interrupted transaction whose `.prune.txn` intent is still present) return one identical signed receipt: an installed same-plan intent is completed to the original `pruned` receipt and a prepared one is rolled back and retried.
